content: The following recommendations are applicable to all adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV: 1. Trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses are authorized to initiate first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART). This recommendation is strongly supported by evidence of moderate certainty. Similarly, these healthcare professionals can also maintain ART for patients, with the same level of evidence and recommendation strength. 2. Trained and supervised community health workers are permitted to dispense ART between regular clinical visits. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. 3. Trained and supervised lay providers are allowed to distribute ART. This recommendation is strong but supported by low-certainty evidence. 4. Task sharing for specimen collection and point-of-care testing with non-laboratory personnel should be implemented in settings with limited professional staffing capacity. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 5. Decentralization of ART care is recommended to improve access and retention in care. Effective approaches include: Initiating ART in hospitals and maintaining it in peripheral health facilities (strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence). Both initiation and maintenance of ART in peripheral health facilities (strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence). Initiating ART at peripheral health facilities and maintaining it at the community level, which includes outreach sites, health posts, home-based services, or community-based organizations (strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence). The frequency of clinic visits should be tailored to the patient’s health status. 6. ART should be initiated and maintained in maternal and child healthcare settings for pregnant and postpartum women and infants. This is a strong recommendation, though based on very-low-certainty evidence. 7. In settings with a high burden of HIV and tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated in TB treatment settings with linkage to ongoing HIV care. Additionally, TB treatment may be provided for people living with HIV in HIV care settings where a TB diagnosis has been made. Both recommendations are strong but supported by very-low-certainty evidence. 8. Sexual and reproductive health services, including family planning and sexually transmitted infection (STI) management, can be integrated into HIV care settings. This is a conditional recommendation with very-low-certainty evidence. Similarly, diabetes and hypertension care may also be integrated into HIV services under the same recommendation strength and evidence certainty. 9. ART should be initiated and maintained for people living with HIV in care settings that provide opioid substitution therapy (OST). This is a strong recommendation with very-low-certainty evidence. 10. Disease programs, particularly for HIV and TB, should work towards balanced integration of diagnostic services. This is a good practice statement. 11. Adolescent-friendly services should be implemented within HIV care to enhance engagement and improve outcomes. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. Community-based approaches can further improve treatment adherence and retention in care for adolescents living with HIV, though this is a conditional recommendation with very-low-certainty evidence. Training healthcare workers can also contribute to better adherence and retention among adolescents (conditional recommendation, very-low-certainty evidence). 12. Adolescents should be counseled on the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV status to others. They should be empowered and supported to decide if, when, how, and to whom they disclose their status. This is a conditional recommendation with very-low-certainty evidence. 13. Psychosocial interventions should be provided to all adolescents and young adults living with HIV. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 14. Electronic communication can be considered to transfer test results and reduce delays in acting on results for infant diagnosis and other essential laboratory tests. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. The World Health Organization (WHO) promotes a public health approach to HIV prevention, treatment, and care, particularly in resource-limited settings. These guidelines consolidate evidence-based recommendations to improve access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) and address structural barriers such as stigma, discrimination, and violence. They emphasize a people-centered approach and aim to strengthen health systems while promoting human rights and gender equity.
